It has been found that they have collected double rates time after time. After the rate has been prepaid along comes the driver representing these express monopolies in the United States and he collects a second rate in many cases. The Americans see that to-day they are carrying the parcel post of foreign countries through their own country for one-third the price they have to pay on parcels shipped by the express monopolies and the people of the United States will not long stand that kind of thing. I do not disagree with the suggestion of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) that this should be made the subject of inquiry by commission, nor do I disagree with the late Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) that further conferences should take place, but I do say that nothing of that kind will be effective; the only way to get at these companies is for us to get into the business ourselves. The new principle of this twentieth century in connection with these great monopolies owned and controlled by private companies is that, if you cannot buy them out at a. fair price you should go into competition with them. They got their franchises giving them the right to operate in the country and that imposed upon them the duty of dealing out fair treatment to the public and of giving the public a reasonable toll. These companies have failed in their obligation to the people and, having failed, the state is justified in going into competition with them. If we cannot have state ownership, let us have state competition. The cost of stringing telegraph wires across this country is comparatively small, the right of way is easily obtained; we have better poles than are to be found in I 131
any other country in the world; we can make the copper wire here if necessary out of our own copper, and indeed telegraph construction in Canada is so cheap that the companies are ashamed to show what it actually costs in comparison with their capitalization. I declare for state competition, and I declare we should start it now. Start it and watch the coon come down and see how quick he will come down when you announce that you are going into the business. As long as they can put us off with promises of concessions, they will do nothing 3erious. Recently, the public did get a concession, and, strange to say, that concession came one week after the discussion I raised in this House. The coon came down to that extent. It did not happen accidentally; I do not claim the credit for it myself, but I claim that the discussion in this House is entitled to that credit. You will get nothing from those monopolies if you merely say you will negotiate with them. Go into the telephone business and give our farmers cheap phones. I heard reference to-night to the case of Manitoba, and no doubt there have been increases there, and that should be so, but I do believe that the people of Manitoba and Saskatchewan and Alberta would not part with their public owned telegraph system on any account.
What are the telephone charges in Manitoba?
I can not give the exact figures, but I know that reductions were made when the province took them over, and we would have reductions in Ontario if we had state-owned telephones.
Has not the price been raised in Manitoba?
Suppose it has?
That is not an answer.
There has been some change in the rate, and the Manitoba government was taunted for not having quite realized what it promised to do.
That is a very mild statement of it.

Well, I will go so far as to admit, if you like, that public ownership in Manitoba has failed, but I will point the hon. gentleman fifty other instances where it has been a great success in other countries.
Name one.
Denmark is one; seven dollars a year for a telephone to every farmer in Denmark.
Why did you not go further for an example?

Because that is the best example of public ownership. There is a gentleman who is ashamed of public ownership; he is ashamed of the people of Canada, and he thinks they are not competent to go into the business and be trusted with public affairs of that kind. I am prepared to trust the Canadian people in connection with public ownership; I am ready to say to the people of Canada., take over the terminal elevators. I am prepared to see the people of Canada handle their railways, and this government has its one opportunity to * make good in regard to public ownership in connection with the Intercolonial railway. There is a great national asset we have. It is based on public ownership. It has not done as well as it could do, but it can be made to do well if it is administered in the public interest.
What do you think they should do about the Intercolonial railway ?

(South York) I would propose to run it as an absolute public proposition, and to extend it to where the traffic is. Bring it into the province of Ontario, and we make it the greatest railway in Canada. Bring it to Toronto and on to the Detroit river. Put it into Winnipeg. I stood in this House 15 years ago, when the late Mr. Blair was Minister of Railways, and when the proposal was made to build the Rainy River railway in connection with the Canadian Northern, and said that the way to increase the railway accommodation of the west was to make that, line a portion of the Intercolonial, to bring the Intercolonial immediately from Montreal to the Georgian bay, there connect it with boats, build a line around the lakes, carry it to Winnipeg, and from there spread it all over the northwest. If that had been done at that time, the Canadian west would have had a state-owned railway that would have solved all problems. The lines would have been laid out in a scientific way, so as to secure the greatest efficiency all over the country. There is not efficiency in any railway system of the west to-day, because too many of the lines parallel one another.
Is not the Intercolonial all right as it is now ?

(South York) It could be much better. What is the one way out of the difficulty in connection with Mr. NESBITT.
the coal strike in England to-day ? There is very little hope of a settlement unless the state takes over the coal business. I do not know that I am such a state socialist as to advocate that, but the people of England are coming pretty close to it. At the beginning of this year all the telephone lines in England went into the British post office, and they are now being administered in connection with it. The people's experience of state-owned telegraphs was so good that they took over the telephones, and they must now go into the cable business. They cannot stop at telegraphs and telephones when the cables remain undealt with. To my mind there is nothing for us to do but to get into the business without delay, and to say that we are going to have a state-owned cable. We ought to pass a resolution to that effect this session, and then you would see how the rates would come down. There would be a threepenny rate for all messages between Canada and England.
Is not free trade a remedy for all these things ?

(South York) Perhaps tlie hon. gentleman can tell us that. There should be a national policy in regard to other things as well as tariffs; but I will not go into that to-night. The more I study this matter in the light of the experience of other countries, the more convinced I am that if you cannot have state ownership, state competition is the one remedy that will bring down tolls. The solution of the northwest railway problem is to put an absolutely state-owned railway in the Canadian west.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Might I remind the hon. member that the question is in regard to cables.
(South York) The hon. gentleman questioned me in regard to state ownership.

May I b'e allowed to say that I quite agree with my hon. friend in his suggestion that we should 'advocate a state-owned cable, and I might have mentioned it in my amendment; but, as it would involve an expenditure of money, I had to avoid it.
I apologize, Mr. Speaker, for trespassing on your good mature, and I will conclude by saying that the way to bring about the reform is to get into the business of state ownership.
Why ?
Because they have no use for it.
Because the rates are too high.

Even if the rates were low, they would not use it. I speak as a business mam. Occasionally I send a cablegram, but it is of very little importance to mie whether we have a state-owned cable line or not, because I use the cable so seldom; and as far as 95 per cent of the people of this country are concerned, I do not believe they 'are at >all interested in cheap cable meissages or in >a state-owned cable. They would not use it and it would be of little or no value to them. The same thing applies to the nationalization of the telegraph lines. How many of the people of this country use the telegraph lines ? I venture to say that 90 per cent of the people of this country do not send one telegram in 12 months. They are of no importance to the farmers of this 'Country. Are the telegraph rates high ? You can send a telegram from the town in which I live to Montreal for 25 cents, and you can send a night letter of I think 50 words for 25 cents.
Is there any general demand for anything cheaper than that? Would it be any great advantage to the people of this country that it should be any cheaper? It may be an advantage to a few people who are interested in telegraph lines to a very great extent, but the great majority ot our people are not interested in the question whatever.
I believe that private capital and enterprise should develop, not only the cable and telegraph lines, but the telephone lines as well. In the county which I represent, rural telephone companies have covered the entire district with telephones. They give the farmers a telephone foT $12 per year, and I doubt very much, if in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, where the province owns thjse lines, the telephone service is as cheap, or any cheaper at any rate, than it is throughout. *he province of Ontario, where local telephone companies have been formed, and are operating efficiently. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this question is of very little importance to the great majority of the people. It may be 131 i
on advantage to the few, but it is not an advantage to the many. Gentlemen who corne from the cities., from the commercial centres, may be interested and they do advocate these schemes in the House from time to time, but let me tell the Postmaster General that the farmers of Canada are interested in something of very much more importance to them than projects of this kind, which hare been brought before the House. They are interested to-day in a rural mail delivery.
Some hon MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

If this government wants to do something in the interest of the farmers, that is a matter which they might properly undertake. The farmers are not even interested so much in the parcel post system concerning which we have heard a great deal. Is there any reason why parcels should be carried from Toronto to Vancouver for the same price as they ;vouid be carried for, from the town in which I live to Toronto? I do not believe the government should go into that business, and compete with the express companies at the same rate throughout the whole of Canada. The former Postmaster General gave the farmers a little taste of what rural mail delivery is like. He adopted a system of rural mail delivery upon the main mail routes, and I want to tell him that the farmers who received their newspapers and letters daily upon these routes are so interested in it, that in other parts of the province-and I can speak more particularly of Ontario than of any other province, because I am more familiar with it-are strongly asking for the benefits or rural mail delivery and they will never be satisfied until they get it.
Hear, hear.

I hope that the Postmaster General and the government will not delay any time in giving to the Ontario farmers a proper system of rural mail delivery. Why should they not have it? The farmers contribute to the revenues of Canada to a very great extent, as we all know. They produce the wealth of this country, and it is upon the farmers that we mainly depend in Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to remind the hon. gentleman that he is wandering from the question, which is that of cable rates.

Perhaps I am a little out of order in discussing the questions of rural mail delivery and telephone nationalization, but if I have trespassed it is because others have trespassed before me. I want to say in conclusion that the farmers want from this government rural mail delivery in preference to any of these fad's

that we have heard discussed in this House from time to time this session.

I would not have said anything on the subject had not the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), made the statement that I was opposed to public ownership, because I asked him a question. I did not say that I was opposed to public ownership, but I do say now that I am opposed to any hon. member taking up the time of the House in talking about some fad, talking in generalities and making a lot of statements in support of which he is not prepared to produce one tittle of evidence. I asked the hon. gentleman a question about Denmark, but I doubt whether he knows anything more about that country than he knows about Manitoba, and that is nothing. Even if they do have rural telephones and telegraphs in Denmark for seven dollars, it does not take very much ol a telegraph line to cover the whole burg. Besides that, I doubt, as I said before, whether he knows anything about what they do in Denmark.
Thank you.
I am opposed to general statements being made without producing facts before a lot of business men such as we are supposed to be in this House.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman talked about cable rates, but he wandered over many subjects, and it is surprising that he did not touch upon aviation before he concluded. He certainly talked a lot about building railways, and1 that has no connection with cables.
Hear, hear.

I would not have spoken if the hon. gentleman had not stated that I was opposed to public ownership. I am opposed to public ownership if it is not carried on in a business way. Talk about carrying a thing for nothing, the state cannot do business for nothing any more than can a private corporation. As a matter of fact in regard to telephones the Manitoba authorities had to arrange their rates.
I did not say they had not done so. I said I admitted1 it.

You said you did not know anything about it, which I can quite believe. I would like to emphatically endorse what my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) said, as to what the farmers are interested in The farmers of Ontario, in common with those of the other provinces, help to pay the taxes and they are Mr. LALOR.
making no grumble over it. They are paying their fair proportion and they would like to share in some of the benefits resulting from the progress of the _ country. I hope the Postmaster General will follow up the policy which was inaugurated by his predecessor and make a point of seeing that the farmers get rural mail delivery in a systematic way.
I would like to say a few words with reference to the motion now before the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has exhausted his right to speak a second time.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, I have not exhausted (my right to speak with reference to the .amendment which the member for Rouvi'lle (Mr. Lemieux) has presented to the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The original motion is for the Speaker to leave the Chair in order that the House may go into Committee of Supply, to which the hon. gentleman has already spoken. An amendment has been moved now, and I think the hon. member having expressed himself on the original motion, it would not be in order for him to speak again.
But this is supposed to be an amendment is it not? Do I understand, Mr. Speaker, that I have not the privilege of speaking to the amendment offered by the member for Rou-ville?

Perhaps I may be allowed to make a suggestion. The motion to go into Committee of Supply was made by the Minister of Finance, and my hon. friend from East Lambton, (Mr. Armstrong) spoke to that without proposing any resolution. Then the member for Rouville presented an amendment to the main motion, and I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that by the rules of the House, a new question is before the House on the amendment. I should therefore, think that the hon. member for East Lambton would have the right to speak.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Following the usual practice, the hon. member would have the right to speak, but, unless my memory is very much in fault, it has been ruled in this House that when a motion is made to go into Committee of Supply, and an hon. gentleman has once spoken, on it, he has not the right to speak again upon an amendment to that motion. Personally, I am not opposed to any hon. member speaking, but I would like as far as possible, to facilitate the work of the House, and keep members within the customary usages. Of course, if it is the pleasure of the House to allow the hon. gentleman to proceed, I have no objection whatever.

With regard to what has been the practice, according to my recollection, in a case of this kind, the member for East Lambton would have a perfect right to speak, but I think he would be obliged to confine himself to the amendment. That is the view I take on the point, and I think it has been so ruled by former Speakers.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: No matter who speaks after the amendment is moved, the rule is, that he should confine himself to the amendment.
That is quite correct, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion.

I understand many members of the House would like to speak on this question and, as I am afraid if the hon. gentleman speaks until six o'clock, the question will be automatically out of the order paper, therefore I would ask the hon. member to move the adjournment.
The hon. gentleman knows full well that that matter was left over and that the following day a portion of it was taken- up by another member of this House and dealt with to a certain extent. A little later I withdrew it from the order paper for the purpose of bringing it up on going into supply and dealing with it definitely, according to the motion I had prepared.
On. the occasion, to which he refers the hon. gentleman himself spoke for three hours on the subject.

Mr. *Speaker, it was not two hours. And if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) could place on ' Hansard ' more definite and useful material for the benefit of those discussing this question, than I did, I should be glad to give way to him. If, instead of bringing in .an academic motion which on the face of it means nothing, the hon. gentleman had fallen in behind the motion which he knew I expected to place before the House, be would have been supporting something worthy of him. That motion would have declared:
That, in the opinion of this House, a commission should he appointed to investigate the systems of National telegraphs and telephones, wireless telegraphs and cables; also postal conditions, laws and regulations, parcel post, means of collecting and distributing mails, with a view to submitting such data and information to the Post Office Department as would help to improve existing conditions in all the above; and to further inquire into postal facilities in rural districts in other countries in order that a better system of ru-al free mail delivery may be inaugurated.
The labours of this commission would result in gathering such facts and figures that even the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) would be satisfied that the House could deal intelligently with these ' fads ,' as the hon. member foT Hal-dimand (Mr. Lalor) chooses to call them. It is not so many years ago since many of these hon. gentlemen looked upon free rural mail delivery as a fad. The day is not far distant when we, as a parliament.

will be compelled to take up these matters and deal with them definitely. Some hon. members seem to think that national organization of the telegraph and telephone is not in the interest of the people of the rural districts. In the figures I gave the House I showed that theTe were 460 independent telephone companies in the province of Ontario at the mercy of a public corporation that was all-powerful. And instead of our being able to control the trunk lines and connect up these independent companies, giving them long distance rates at cost, these hon. gentlemen are glad to have this concern make the amount of money out of this service that it is making at the present time.
However, I do not wish to take up more time. I have only to say that I am surprised at the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) not being generous enough to allow me to read the motion which I expected, and which he fully knew I expected and intended, to place before the House this evening.
Hon. Mr. PUGS'LEY.	I believe I
express the opinion of the majority if not of all the members here present when I say that my hon, friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) has no reason whatever to find fault with the hon. member for Eouville (Mr. Lemieux). The hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) concluded his remarks and took his seat without presenting his motion to the House. My hon. friend from Eouville had every reason to believe that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) did not intend to make a motion. So that it was quite in order for my hon. friend from Eouville to make his remarks and to submit his resolution to the House.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Did not I refer several times to the motion I intended to move? And in starting out did not I distinctly state that I was bringing forward the notice of motion to whicv' I had referred some weeks ago in the form of a motion to be placed before the House?

I was here during a portion of the time my hon. friend was speaking, and certainly I was not impressed with the idea, when he got through with his speech, that he had forgotten anything. I thought he had entirely concluded his speech and done all he intended to do in presenting his views to the House. Then it was quite in order for my hon. friend from Eouville (Mr. Lemieux) to present his motion, after the conclusion of his speech; and it would have been entirely out of order for him to allow his motion to stand and a motion made by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) to take its place. The hon. member for East Mr. AEMSTEONG (E. Lambton).
Lambton no doubt unfortunately forgot to make his motion; but that is an accident which may happen to any of us. He may have been a little excited at the moment, his memory may have been overwhelmed by the importance of the subject he was dealing with, and consequently he forgot the important thing-in his own estimation -of submitting his motion to the House. He complains of the amendment of my hon. friend from Eouville as being academic. Well, it is not academic beyond what every private member of this House may say on a subject when he has no power of making a proposition which would involve the expenditure of public money. All my hon. friend could do was to move that in the opinion of this House it was desirable that the cable rates should be still further lowered, and urging the Postmaster General to take steps to that end. That is substantially the motion which I have great pleasure in seconding.
Now during the discussion, remarks have been made in favour of the government proceeding at once to establish a istate-owned cable. I do not wish to be understood, in seconding this motion, as committing myself to the principle of a state-owned cable at the present time. The time may come, and may come sooner perhaps than most of us expect, when it may be in the public interest to establish a state-owned cable, but I do not think that time has yet arrived. The cable companies have responded I think very well to the public demand for a reduction, and they have made a considerable reduction. But if the reduction is not sufficient in the opinion of this government, they have the remedy in their own hands. There are two at least of the cable lines which have their Atlantic termini in Canada, I think more than two. As to those companies at all events having their Atlantic termini in Canada this parliament can legislate, this parliament hag, power to place their "tolls and rates under the 'control of the Board of Bailway Commissioners	who can determine	whatshould be fair and proper rates to allow, just the same as they are now able to control railway rates. It does seem to me that before this country plunges into a very large expense for the establishment of a new cable line, an effort ought to be made to bring these cable companies which have their Atlantic termini in Canada, under the control of the board of Bailway	Commissioners In	1910 an	Actwas	-passed	which made	provision	thatthe	Board	of Eailway	Commissioners
should have control of the rates of cable companies connected with land lines in Canada, and by section 6 of that Act it was provided that the Act should come into force upon similar provision being made by the proper authority in the

United Kingdom and upon proclamation by the Governor in Council. Now it would appear that the government of Great Britain has taken no action towards providing similar legislation. It seems to me that my hon. friend the Postmaster General should communicate with the Imperial authorities upon'the subject, and if they decide that they will not take action along me lines taken by this parliament, then this parliament ought to strike out section 6 of the statute and act upon its own account, act on behalf of the people of Canada, and make provision that in respect of these cable companies their rates must be such as the Board of Railway Commissioners may think reasonable. I think in that way the people of Canada could be assured of reasonable and fair tolls. But before that experiment is tried, without trying the experiment of having these tolls submitted to the Board of Railway Commissioners, I for one would' not be prepared to give any encouragement to the proposition to go to the very large expenditure which would be involved in the establishment and operation of a cable system to be owned by the state.
Reference has been made to a state-owned cable on the Pacific ocean. Now I asked the hon. member for Toronto, how the cable rates upon the Pacific compared with the rates established by the cable companies on the Atlantic, and he stated, I think correctly, that the cable rates from land to land are higher, but the distances are greater, and that it would not be fair to compare the rates arbitrarily without taking into account the distances. But it must be borne in mind that the ocean distance ought not to be a governing factor, because wnen a cable is once laid there are no stations to be maintained on the ocean, there are no expenses to be borne at all except the ordinary expenses of making repairs from time to time. Therefore, one could not expect that the cable rates upon the Pacific would be, in proportion to the distance, so much greater than the rates upon the Atlantic. Whether a cable is owned by a company or whether it is owned by the state, certain tolls must be charged. It cannot be expected that the government would operate a cable at a great loss to the people at large; because, as has been remarked by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor), it is only a small proportion of the public who use these cables. Reference has been made by the hon. member for Toronto to what he calls excessive telegraph rates. I agree with the hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the subject, that the public has reason, I think, not to be too severe upon the telegraph companies so far as their operations on the land are concerned. I think
the reductions which they have made recently in rates have been reasonable and fair reductions. As he has stated, telegrams can be sent for long distances in Canada at 25 to 30 cents, and lately provision has been made for night lettergrams, which are very cheap indeed, and are found to be a great convenience. I do not wish to take up any more time of the House. I only desired to call attention to the statute we have on the subject, and to suggest to the Postmaster General, if he would allow me to do so, that it might not be inopportune to communicate with the Imperial authorities with a view of suggesting legislation along the same lines as this parliament legislated in 1910; and if the British government decline to take any action, then he should consider the repeal of section 6, and1 allow the Board of Railway Commissioners to deal with the regulation of the rates and tolls of the cable companies which have land lines in Canada.

I regret that my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), has not been able to put his motion in your hands.
My hon. friend has given to this matter such careful attention, he has gone into his subject so fully that I think the country is indebted to him for the numerous facts he has disclosed. I am of opinion that there is a great deal in what he has said which would turn out to be in the public interest. The hon. member for Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux) has told him he spoke too long. I do not think he has spoken one minute too long. In the whole course of his remarks he has not repeated one thing, he has placed hard facts before us and every hon. member who has heard him has learned something. The rules of the House prevent me from going at any length into the different matters in his original motion except perhaps by way of comparison. I may say to my hon. friend that after hearing his speech of the other day I read it in ' Hansard ' and that the ' Hansard ' of that day has been put on file in the department as a most valuable piece of information. I might suggest that after his instructive speech the commission he wanted to have appointed becomes almost unnecessary because I do not think any commission could give us more information than he has given us in the speech he has made.
As the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) has said the motion of the hon. member for Rouville is an academic one. I shall not go so far as to say that the hon. member for Rouville has put this motion before the House just for the sake of having the glory of starting this debate; I think his motives are higher than that.

But there is not much in the motion. The steps which the hon. member speaks of in the motion have been taken and I would like the country to believe that my hon. friend has advanced nothing very new tonight. He has gone on the lines on which the Post Office Department has been working for months so I think everybody should keep what belongs to him. What we have we will hold.
I am glad this matter has been brought before the House because it has given the hon. members on both sides an opportunity of discussing this very important question. The matter of cable rates has engaged the attention of preceding governments. It has been the subject of discussion in Imperial Conferences and I am of opinion that it is most important for this country that we secure reasonable cable rates. I have already said and in that I concur with the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) that there are other things which are more pressing in this country than cheap cable rates. I have said that I was in hopes before long that we would be able to place before the House a system of rural mail delivery which to my mind was much more important than the other subjects mentioned to-night. . I am happy to say that since I then spoke I have had occasion and opportunity of putting before my colleagues in the government this question of rural delivery with the intention of placing it on a more businesslike basis, with less duplication, in short of having something which will appeal to the people afid will serve them better than the existing loose system. I will have occasion before many d^ys to ask the concurrence of this House in the creation of a special branch in the department to attend to this rural mail delivery for which the people are asking. It will cost some little money but the government have come to the conclusion that it will be money well spent. I am bound to say that we shall not go by leaps and bounds in this new policy. We shall have the counties mapped out in a regular way, so as to spend as little money as possible and to have at the same time as complete a service as possible. We shall have to take this matter up carefully and our friends in this House will have to understand that we will not be able to go into all the counties, that we must proceed by degrees and look ahead of us, not look at a particular township or parish, but at what is going to be the route to be followed from the point where we cease work this year and will begin next year, so as to have the whole thing arranged on a businesslike plan.
We have been told that the rural free mail delivery is in great demand. I Mr. PELLETIER
believe in it, the government believes in it, and we will do our best to give the people of this country this rural mail delivery. It will help the people to read more, to know more, to educate themselves, to communicate with one another more frequently, and I think on the whole it will be considered that this government has conferred a boon on the people of this country. This, in my humble opinion, was the first question we had to take up. We are going to do so this session. As to the other points, we will be unable to look into them sufficiently to be able to propose any policy during the course of the present session. During the recess I shall take all the time at my disposal to go very carefully into this question to give every one of these questions mature consideration, and whilst I agree with the hon. member for Haldimand that rural mail delivery is of far more importance than these other matters, because it will give benefits to more people, I do not entirely agree with him as to the cheapness of cable and telegraph rates.
I do not attribute the fault to any particular company, but I am sorry as a Canadian, that our friends in Winnipeg have to get their European news through St. Paul and Minneapolis, and that the citizens of Vancouver have to get their European news through Seattle. If there is any way by which the Canadian people can get news from the old country over telegraph lines on Canadian territory, and through British sources, we will endeavour to bring that condition about. If we succeed in that. I think we will have accomplished something to promote the best interests of all Canada. I believe the telegraph rates are too high; I go so far as to say, they are excessive. We have been told that the farmers do not use the cable and that is true, but the trade of the country uses the cable, and the trade of the country exists for the benefit of the farmers just as well as for any other class, and as the policy of this government is to trade with England, we should have a cheap means of quick communication with the mother country with which we desire to trade. A cheap cable system is one of the missing links in our trade relations with Britain, and we must, in my opinion, do cur utmost to make some progress towards attaining it. On the 4th of March there will be a sitting of the Board of Railway Commissioners m Winnipeg to inquire into some of these important questions and I have appointed counsel to represent my department and to ascertain for us if the telegraph rates are actually excessive. It may be that there is a combine to keep up these rates, and although we are sometimes taunted with being a government of com-

bines, we have in this case, appointed counsel to attend this investigation in the interests of the public, and to place a report (before the House. To the extent that if it is found that the telegraph rates are excessive, I can assure the House that we will come to the relief of the people. I very much regret to say that I have no very great encouragement to give the country to-night as to the redaction in cable rates.
I do not wish to say anything in criticism of the Postmaster General of England, but I am bound to give the facts to this House.
I am in almost constant correspondence with the right hon. Mr. Samuel, and I regret to say that he feels that we should not go any further at present in the direction indicated in the correspondence. I repeat my expression of regret at the attitude taken by Mr. Samuel. I have here an official letter, which I received from the right hon. gentleman lately, and the contents of which I shall communicate to the House. It is as follows:
General Post Office, London,
- 7th February, 1912.
Dear Mr. Pelletier,-In reply to your letter of the 8th ultimo, I need hardly say that I share your view as to the benefits of cheap cable rates.
While, however, I recognize in this connection the advantages which might be expected from a state-owned Atlantic cable, they are, in my opinion, outweighed by the fact that, under present conditions, such a cable would hardly be self-supporting, so that if one were laid any considerable reduction of rates could only be effected at the expense of the general taxpayers. As you are perhaps aware I spoke in some detail on this aspect of the matter during the discussion at the Imperial Conference in the last year.
Since the conference the position has changed in two ways-the projected combination of three of the Trans-Atlantic Cable Companies has become a fact and the reductions in cable rates I foreshadowed have been brought into operation. I do not think that we need regard these reductions as final. No doubt in due course further concessions may be expected without incurring the heavy expense of laying a government cable. This point was touched on in an answer by me in the House of Commons on the 12th of December last of which, as it deals also with the strategic argument for the cable, I inclose a copy.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) HERBERT SAMUEL. Hon. L. P. Pelletier, M.P.
The following are the remarks made by Mr. Samuel in the Imperial House of Commons and which are referred to in his letter:
There are thirteen cables from the United Kingdom to North America and all of them land on Canadian or Newfoundland territory This fact should be borne in mind in connection with the strategic considerations raised by the hon. member's question.
The land lines both in Canada and the United States are in the hands, not of the governments, but of private companies, .and there is no guarantee under existing conditions that a state-owned cable, if laid, would be able to establish connections with the land lines in those countries. On this side, the British Post Office would not be able to supply the cable with such traffic, as the Anglo-American Cable Company is entitled, under an old agreement, to receive all trans-Atlantio cablegrams which are not ordered by the senders to be transmitted by a specified route. The business of the Pacific Cable Board is at present far from sufficient to justify laying an additional cable across the Atlantic in order to carry its traffic alone.
The hon. member's question is inaccurate in that it suggests that all the trans-Atlantic cable system is now under the control of one corporation. The Commercial Cable Company with five cables is not a party to the combination recently formed.
I have established, as a condition of the renewal or transfer of landing licenses, government control of the rates charged by some of the cable companies, and shall extend this control as the licenses of others fail to be renewed. VVhere the control applies rates cannot be raised without the consent of the government, and may be reduced on the demand of the government. The companies have a right of appeal to the Railway and Canal Commissioners if the equity of any proposed reduction is disputed.
In view of all these circumstances and of the substantial reductions now being made in many of the trans-Atlantic rates, His Majesty's government has no present intention of embarking on the large capital expenditure and annual commitments which would be involved in laying a state-owned cable.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that if the right hon. Mr. Samuel has the right, as he undoubtedly has, to practically control the rates, the self-governing colonies of the empire have the right to ask him that those rates shall be so controlled that Canada and the other selfgoverning colonies will not be forced to pay excessive charges. As Postmaster General of Canada I have answered Mr. Samuel, asking him to use his authority to promise easy and cheap communication between the mother country and Canada. I do not think it will be necessary to have a state-owned cable. There are many heavy demands on the public treasury of Canada and in this young country we have to expend a great deal of money to keep pace with the progress of the times*, so that if we can dispense with the expenditure on a state-built cable, the money thus saved could very well be applied elsewhere. I trust that the Postmaster General of England will before long be able to see eye to eye with us on this matter. We desire, as I have said, to trade with the mother country and in order to carry on that trade with

facility we must have cable communication at the cheapest cost possible.
We do not object to have communication with other countries, but this country prefers to have communication in all forms with England. Of course, the day may come, and the day will come, when the mother country will have some kind of reciprocal relations with the colonies. It is not the business of my department to go into the question of reciprocal trade relations ; but we want the government of England and its Postmaster General to help the trade of this country. The British preference has been put on the Statute-book in order that we may have more trade with England, and if we trade with England we have to communicate with England. Business men will not send pressing orders for what they want to buy in England, by means of letters. They have to use the cable, and it seems to me that it would be very much to the interest of both countries that this should be done. If it is not done, this government will have to look into the question. I am not going an" further than that; I am not- authorized to go any further; but I will go as far as to say that the government will look into the question seriously. There is one fact more to which I will briefly refer before resuming my seat. Most of these cable companieg land in Canada or in Newfoundland. They are controlled by foreign capital. I see no reason why there should not be one cable, [DOT]owned by a company of British subjects. I do not object to our neighbours to the south investing their money in this country; on the contrary, I am prepared to invite that; but I think that Canada and England will both desire to have a cable company, and a cable that would not be controlled by foreign capital. I am not prepared to-night to go into this matter at any great length; but the House will, I think, be of opinion that these questions may -well engage the attention of hon. members. I would ask my hon. friend not to press his motion, which I think is too academic, and not practical enough.
In what sense?

It is going to be published in the newspapers, and the people who Tead it will say: This gentleman does rot seem to attach much importance to this matter, as he .makes a motion of fine words, but no action.
On the contrary, I ask for action.
The hon. gentleman says he hopes that steps will be taken, as if steps were not taken now.
Go further.
Steps were taken before the hon. gentleman made his motion,

so that I do not see that there is any occasion for it. I do not wish to divide the House on the motion; I would prefer to have the hon. gentleman withdraw it. Under the circumstances, it would have no good effect. The Post Office Department is giving its full attention to this matter, and I do not think there is any necessity of saying that we should take steps. We have done so and will do so, without being invited in any academic way to blow' our trumpet.

SUPERIOR COURT JUDGE IN OTTAWA COUNTY.
speechtext: Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Justice if the statement made by Mr. Justice McDougall yesterday at Hull while presiding over the court was true, that he had interviewed the Minister of Justice and that a new judge was to be appointed at Hull.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SUPERIOR COURT JUDGE IN OTTAWA COUNTY.
speechtext:
I have not seen the statement of Mr. Justice McDougall, but the Quebec Legislature has provided for a new judicial district to toe called Montcalm, and that until there is a proper court house at the Chef-lieu of Montcalm district, the judge to be appointed shall reside at Hull. It is the intention when we introduce the Bill to provide for the additional judges which are asked for by the different provinces to make provision for the salary of the judge which the legis-ture has determined is required for the
district of Montcalm, and who is to pre side at Hull, and that was so stated to the Hon. Mr. Justice McDougall.

['So I understood. Then we will take up other Bills as far as it may be convenient to hon. members on the other side, and then resume in Supply, with the estimates of the Minister of Railways and Canals.\nMotion agreed to and the House adjourned at 12.55 a. m. Friday.', 'Friday, March 1, 1912.']
What supply is to be taken up?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Railways and canals.

The Premier knows it has always been the custom previous to going into Committee of Supply on the estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals for the minister to give to the House a statement with reference to the transportation problems of the country generally, and particularly with reference to the Intercolonial railway, and that course has facilitated the passage of Supply. In my recollection in parliament, this is the first time in which it has been proposed to take up Supply on railways and canals without having a statement of that kind. I am quite sure the minister will agree with me in that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not agree that the practice has been invariable.

Well, if not invariable, it has been the custom during the last eight years, ever since I have been in the House. The questions involved in regard to railway matters, of necessity, require that there should be some statement as to the position of the Intercolonial railway to begin with. It enables hon. members in considering Supply to have beforehand information in succinct form which otherwise could not be elicited except by prolonged questioning.

I agree with cmy right hon. friend from Pictooi that it will no doubt facilitate the business of the House if a general statement could be made by the minister, prior to taking up the railway estiim'atgs. For example, the financial condition of the Intercolonial railway is watched with a great deal of interest by the members of this House as well as by the people of the country. During the time that I have had the honour of a seat in this House it has been the invariable practice for the Minister of Railways to open the consideration of the railway estimates by making suich a statement, which has been regarded as only second in importance to the budget speech of the Finance Minister. I think it would be a mistake to do away with that very laudable practice. Not only do we want to know what has happened in regard to the Intercolonial railway and what the prospects are for the future business year, but we wouild like to be favoured with some information in regard to the deepening of the Welland cand, the deep-

ening of the Georgian Bay carnal, the conr stiuiotion of the Hudson Bay railway, and other matters. lA.11 these questions are looming np and it certainly would he important for the House to be in possession of a general statement setting forth the policy of the government in regard to these great transportation problems.

I think also, Mr. Chairman,-I do not know whether it was justifiable or not-that there was a general opinion upon this side of the House that if we went into Supply to-night the estimates of the Minister of the Interior would be taken up. I trust the Prime Minister will, particularly as tire hour is quite late, yield to the view that there should be a statement made by the Minister of Railways. Where such a practice has been resorted to year after year for a great many years, we ooone to look upon it almost as the law of parliament. I think that for some ten or twelve years past there never has been an occasion when the House has gone into consideration of the railway estimates without a statement having first been made by the Minister of Railways. But perhaps my hon. friend would even now give us that statement. If not, I am sure that we on this side would cheerfully allow him one day far further preparation in order to make that statement to-morrow. But, speaking seriously, I really do not think my right hon. -friend (Mr. Borden) would be wise in making so radical a departure from what has been the custom during the last ten, twelve, perhaps fifteen, years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I can only say that since the House went into committee and up to the present time, my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) has not had much opportunity of making a statement. Further than that, hon. members on the other side seem to be so much impressed with the value of speech that they insist that we shall talk whether we want to or not. I suppose the Minister of Railways and Canals must be permitted to explain his estimates in the way that seems best to himself. It is true that it has been the practice, particularly under the late Minister of Railways and Canals to make a statement explaining the general condition of the Intercolonial railway. It- may be that that course has its advantages in some respects, but I do not know that there is any absolutely inflexible rule that it shall be done on all occasions. As to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers) he was here in the early part of the evening but has been obliged to leave. If the House had gone into Supply a little earlier his estimates would have been taken up. But we wish to make a little progress. I would suggest Mr. SINCLAIR.
that we might go on and hon. gentlemen can get the information that is available in the way that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) who is in charge of tihe department prefers to give it.

Hon members who are interested in the Intercolonial railway did not know that we were going into the Intercolonial railway estimates to-night, and a good many hon. members are not here who would like to be present when these estimates are taken up. Under the circumstances it seems hardly fair to ask us to go on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What department would hon memhers like to take up?
The House understood that we were going on with the estimates of the Interior Department until they were finished.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps we could take up canals.
I do not know. Our friends from Ontario who are interested in canals are not here.
I was certainly under the impression that we were to go on with the Department of the Interior.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That would have been taken up but for the circumstance to which I have alluded.

If my hon. friend is determined to go into railway estimates tonight, I think this would be a very proper time to get some information with regard to one of the branch lines of the Intercolonial railway.
