member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) is not present-
Mr.. MACDONALD. If my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) will pardon me for a moment -the vote of which this is one item amounts to $4,158,350. Surely, the Prime Minister and Minister of Railways and Canals can hardly expect to get that vote through to-night. The discussion will necessarily he long.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is there any other item hon. gentlemen opposite would like to take up?

I may explain to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways that, as he is no doubt aware from the papers on file in the department, an agreement was
[DOT]4125

made by the ex-Minister of Railways with the Salisbury and Harvey Railway Company some time during the past summer- the exact date will appear from the letter which the ex-Minister of Railways wrote to the president of that railway company. In that letter the ex-minister referred to certain negotiations whirih had taken place with regard to supplying a -quantity of rails, bridge girders and [DOT]other material for a portion of that railway with a view to its being reopened and put in satisfactory operation. In that letter Mr. Graham, the ex-minister, referred to an offer which the company had made to either sell its railway for a sum of money which the company had stated and which is referred to in the letter, or else to lease the road upon terms which bad been presented to the government by a committee of the different branch railways in the maritime provinces. In the letter the ex-minister states that if these terms are acceded to by the company, legislation will be introduced at the then coming session of parliament-that is, the present session-for the purpose of carrying out the arrangement. Now, as I nave said, I regret that my hon. friend from Kings and Albert is not present. But he will read my remarks in ' Hansard ' and will have an opportunity at a later date of making any comment on them that he may desire to make. That hon. gentleman is reported to have made a public statement not long ago in the province of New Brunswick with regard to the railway which certainly is of a very serious character, and reflects so severely not only upon the ex-Minister of Railways, but upon myself and every other member of the government who had anything to do with the arrangements as to require that the facts should be placed on * Hansard,' so that they may go to the country and particularly to that part of New Brunswick the people of which are so intensely interested in this railway and who were for some months before the arrangements were completed, exceedingly anxious that steps should be taken for the opening up of the portion of the railway which had been closed. I find that the hon. member for Kings and Albert is reported in the St. John ' Standard ' as having made a speech at a banquet given to him in the county of Albert. The date is the 14th of November, 1911. This is the report of his remarks:
' The people of Albert county were fooled about the railway. Promises were made by our opponents that were not intended to be fulfilled. Some oar-loads of rails were sent to Salisbury a day or so before the elections and these were to be taken back again in case the government were defeated. There had been no authority for these rails to be loaded or removed from Moncton, and as soon as the elections were over and the government was defeated, arrangements were made to withdraw these rails. I found it necessary to go to Ottawa. I found out that there had been no contract signed or executed in regard to rails for the Salisbury and Albert railway. I made arrangements for those rails and got them forwarded. Then there was trouble about the bridges. I again went to Ottawa and got the bridges, and I have the authority for saying to you that one of these bridges is now on the line and on the 1st December the road will again be in operation its entire length.
Now, my hon. friend will, I am sure, do me the justice to look up the record, and he will find that a bona fide arrangement was made for the delivery of these rails to that railway company. I think you will agree with me, Mr. Chairman, that the charge which the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler), has made, that it was never intended bona fide to deliver these rails, and that after the government was defeated an order was given to take the rails back, as carrying out the intention which' the government had to deceive the people-that is a charge of a very serious character, and before a member of the House should make a charge so serious, he ought to have all the- facts fully in his possession, and to have the strongest possible justification to make such a charge. Now, I find on looking at the file which the Minister of Railways brought down in answer to my motion, that after that letter of the late Minister of Railways to the company agreeing to their terms, either for the purchase, at a price which was agreed upon, or for the leasing, and engaging to submit legislation at the present session, the matter was followed up by order in council, and an agreement was drawn up by the Department of Justice and submitted in due course to the railway company for signature. ' I happen to know personally, because I had some conferences with Mr. Raymond, who I think, was then the legal partner of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, upon the subject of this agreement. The company had by their telegram, or letters from the manager, agreed to execute a contract. There was, however, some delay, and Mr. Raymond went to the city of New York where he saw the president of the railway company; and as the matter was somewhat urgent by Teason of people being deprived of railway facilities, it was understood1 that Mr. Raymond would wire to me, as the minister representing New Brunswick in the government, and who had taken an active part in endeavouring to get this line of railway opened-it was understood he would wire to me when the contract was signed. After he had gone to New York I received a telegram from him that the contract had been signed by the company, and it was understood that

wfaen it was signed he would1 send it forward to the Deputy Minister of .Railways at Ottawa. I took it for granted that that would be done, and I immediately wired either to the Minister of Railways or to the Deputy Minister of Railways, stating that the contract had been signed and forwarded to-Ottawa, and, asking him to give directions for the delivery of the rails. The department was acting in good faith upon my assurance which I received from Mr. Raymond that the contract had been executed by the company. The contract was dated some time in September, I think. Later on, and after a quantity of rails had been placed upon the cars at Moncton and sent forward for delivery to the railway company, it appeared that Mr. Raymond had neglected to have the contract sent to Ottawa. I remember being in Ottawa after the election, and my attention was called to the matter. I may say that the Minister of Railways made no change in the arrangement by reason of the result of |he election, and everything was going forward just as it had been before the election took place, so far as the delivery of the rails was concerned. On the 5th of October I was informed by Mr. Pottinger, the general manager of the Intercolonial, that the contract had not been received. I find that on the file there is a letter from Mr. Pottinger to Mr. Burpee which I will read:
Moncton, October 5, 1911. T. C. Burpee, Esq.,
Please stop at onoe the delivery of rails and other materials to the Salisbury and Albert railway, as the signed agreement has not yet been received at Ottawa. Please let me know quickly what materials and quantity of each have been delivered.
Yours truly,

Then upon the same day, when I had been informed by Mr. Pottinger that the agreement had not been received1, I wired to Mr. Raymond calling his attention to his assurance that the contract would be at once forwarded to Ottawa, and I received this telegram, a very extraordinary telegram.
St. John, N.B., October 5, 1911. Hon. Wm. Pugsley,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa, Ont.
Expect to make another arrangement with new government.	.

To which I replied as follows:
Ottawa, October 5, 1911.
E. P. Raymond,
St. John, N. B.
You must see it is not a question of making another arrangement with new government, hut of carrying out in good faith arrangement made and under which some rails have been Mr. PUGSLEY.
delivered. You distinctly agreed to send' signed agreement to Ottawa, and wired me that it was signed by company. This was clearly for purpose of letting me know that the matter was complete so far as company was concerned.
(Sgd.) WM. PUGSLEY.
Then later, on the 10th of October, I wrote to the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals as follows:
Ottawa, October 10, 1911.
A. W. Campbell Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, Ottawa.
Some days ago, when I was informed by Mr. Pottinger and yourself that Mr. Raymond had not sent the agreement re Salisbury Harvey Railway, I wired him to do so, and received the reply hereto annexed. My ans-swer is also annexed hereto. I am greatly surprised at the fact of Mr. Raymond not having sent you the agreement, but if the company accepted any of the rails, they could he compelled to carry out the agreement the 6ame as if they had sent it to you-I am, yours truly,
(Sgd.) WM. PUGSLEY.
Now, when my hon. friend, the present Minister of Railways, came into office he would see these letters on file, and would see that the delay in countermanding the ord'er for delivery of rails was due entirely to the fact that the agreement had not been signed, and not, as the hon. member for Kings and Albert told the electors, that it was in pursuance of a design to make the people believe before the election that the rails would be delivered, and then to have them sent back to Moncton after the election. I am satisfied the Minister of Marine and Fisheries could not have known the condition of the agreement, could not have known what Mr. Raymond had1 promised; because I find that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries sent a telegram on the 12th of October to the Minister of Railways and Canals as follows:
St. John, N.B., October 2, 1911 Hon. Frank Cochrane,
Minister of Railways,
Chateau Frontenac, Que.
Agreement made with late government to supply rails and girders to Salisbury and Albert railway to repair their railway pending the agreement to take over railways by government. Since government resigned management refuses to give any further rails. Kindly instruct Pottinger at Moncton to continue supplying sufficient rails and girders so work can he completed. Will see you in Ottawa Tuesday.
(Sgd.) J. D. HAZEN.
I make no complaint of the telegram sent by the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It was a very proper request for him to make as the delivery had been stopped, but I take it for granted that my hon. friend did not know the circumstances under which delivery had been stopped.

On October 14, the Minister of Railways replied to the Minister of Marine as follows:
Ottawa, Oot. 14, 1911.

Hazen,
St. John, N.B.
Message received re 'Salisbury and Albert railway. I find upon inquiry that the company has not executed the agreement they promised to, and which it was said they had done. This is reason, I am informed, for non-delivery more rails and girders.
(Sgd.) F. COCHRANE.
It was only about October 26 that the present Minister of Railways was informed that the contract which I had been informed by Mr. Raymond, had been executed in New York in September, had been delivered to the department and thereupon orders were immediately given by the department to resume the delivery of rails in accordance with the original understanding. I think when my hon. friend the member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) reads these different telegrams, which are all on file in the department, he will come to the conclusion that he did the late Minister of Railways and Canals and myself a great wrong when he charged that the order for delivering these rails had been countermanded after the election simply because the election had gone as it did and that there was never any bona fide intention of delivering these rails. The circumstances are simply as the correspondence discloses. There was the bona fide agreement to deliver the rails. There was the telegram from the solicitor of the company to me that the contract had been signed and the understanding was that it was to be forwrarded immediately to Ottawa. I was advised that the contract was signed, I so informed the department and acting upon that in good faith they gave instructions for the delivery of the material to the railway company. Afterwards, on October 5, they learned that the contract had not been delivered at Ottawa as they had been led to believe it was in course of delivery and for that reason the order for the delivery of the rails and girders was countermanded. Later on, on October 26, when the contract wrns signed as it had been agreed it should be, the present Minister of Railways gave the order for the continuation of the delivery of rails. The hon. member for Kings and Albert not only charges me with bad faith in the matter but he takes to himself all the credit for having obtained the order for the resuming of the delivery of these rails, whereas, as a matter of fact, the order was given when the agreement originally made with the company and which was understood would be executed and forwarded to Ottawa, was actually forwarded in order to protect the department and compel the company to carry out its arrangement.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals will see that by the agreement, legislation is to be obtained during the present session. Unless the legislation is so obtained or unless there is a waiver of that upon the part of the company, I would ask my hon. friend whether it is not worthy of consideration if the company might not say:	Oh, .the government has not carried
out its part of the agreement, it has not obtained the legislation authorizing it either to acquire or to lease the road, and might not the company take a position with regard to payment for the rails which might be detrimental to the public interest?
T think myself, that unless there is some waiver on the part of the company the obligation would be on the government to ask parliament to enact the legislation this session which is provided for in the agreement.

In reply I would say that these rails were shipped before the elections, they were shipped before the contract was signed, but after the department found out that the rails had been shipped, and the contract not signed, they gave orders that the rails should not be unloaded, but should be kept there, and they were not returned to Moncton, they were held there until the contract was signed. I do not know anything about the speech made by the hon. member for Kings and Albert, but I think the hon. member from St. John, (Mr.Pugsley)is wrong in his interpretation of the agreement, As I remember it, they are to pay for these rails, if we do not take over the road, and if we do take over the road, it is to be deducted from the arrangement. So it is unnecessary for us to pass any legislation in reference to it this session.
It has been announced in this House that the promises about the branch lines will be gone into during the vacation, and all those [DOT] that are in the interest of the Intercolonial railway and of the county will be taken over on a fair and equitable basis.
My hon. friend does not mean to have the committee believe that the order stopping delivery of the Tails was made after he came into office, it was made before he came into office.
No, I did not say that.

The hon. gentleman's remarks might be open to that interpretation. The order was made some five days before the late government resigned, and because the arrangement which Mr. Raymond wired me, had been executed had not been delivered to the department,
Would the minister state the surplus of the Intercolonial railway on the 31st January last?
About $700,000. That is within $5,000 of the exact amount.
What will be the surplus at the end -of the financial year?

That is a matter that v. ould be purely guesswork. It depends largely on the cost of running trains or how many snowstorms we have, etc. The hon. member knows the weather conditions have a lot to do with the net profits, but we will not be far out when we say about $600,000 or $700,000.

My hon. friend
should have known before asking the committee to pass the estimates, exactly what the surplus was on January 31, and now at the beginning of the last month of the financial year, he could give us the probable financial results on the 31st of March. I would like the minister before we discuss this matter again, to give us the fullest explanation of what the financial position of the road is, and what it is expected it will be.
The Auditor has just told me that the exact amount up to the 31st of January is $677,000.

The minister can, without much trouble, tell us what the estimated surplus on the 31st of March will be. There are certain expenditures which can be estimated pretty accurately, the only uncertain element being as to the extent of snowstorms and the cost of removal of snow. Such information as that should be given us in order to discuss the future policy with regard to the Intercolonial railway. Without anticipating what I will say at a future date, I have no hesitation in saying in this House now, as I have said before, that the Intercolonial has no business to have a surplus.
Do you think it has?

Well, we would like a statement from the minister in regard to that. I have said the same thing to other ministers who were friendly to me politically. I say that every dollar that is reported as a surplus on the Intercolonial railway means so much money taken out of the pockets of the people of the Maritime provinces, and for no good. When you come to deal with the Intercolonial, you are not dealing with a corporate entity such as a private railway company, which at the end of its financial year has so much money, and as to which the directors can consider whether it will be spent in betterments or whether it will be paid in dividends, because, at the end of the financial year if the Intercolonial has a surplus of eight or nine hundred thousand dollars, that money passes into the treasury of the Dominion, Mr. MACDONALD.
away from the Intercolonial, and not a dollar of it is available for running expenses of the railway for the new year. And then, when the people interested in the line press on the minister for increased accommodation or for improved freight rates, the answer is that the surplus of the previous year has passed away from him and has gone into the general treasury, and there is no money left for these betterments. Before we discuss these estimates again 1 wish the minister would give us the result of the operations of the Intercolonial in the way of surpluses for the last three years, and a statement down to date, so far as he has it, and an estimate up to the 31st of March, in so far as it is possible to anticipate. In certain portions of Canada the feeling is that if a Minister of Railways is able to report a surplus on the Intercolonial he has achieved some distinguished feat, for which he is entitled to credit. I do_ not hesitate to say to the Minister of Railways at the inception of his career as minister, as I have said to my own political friends when they occupied the office, that if a Minister of Railways has a surplus on the Intercolonial, it is not to his credit but to his discredit, for the reason that he has discriminated against the people of the maritime provinces in making them pay more than they had necessity to pay.

There will be no objection to bringing down the statement which the hon. gentleman asks for in reference to the surplus on the Intercolonial for the last three years, and also an estimate of the operations of the road up to the 31st of March. In some aspects of the remarks of the hon. member for Pie-tou I thoroughly agree. Of course, it is a question in my own mind whether this is really a surplus or not. It is a question in my mind whether the betterments on the rolling stock have been kept up from year to year in the manner I think they should have been before there is any surplus claimed. I am having a stocktaking made of the Intercolonial railway, especially with reference to the rolling stock, so as to get at some basis on which we can start anew. I also think that the Intercolonial can be so managed that it will not only pay its way but that it will pay . for betterments as well, and that without raising the present rates. I think I can say, without fear of contradiction, that the rates on the Intercolonial are lower than on any other railroad of the same mileage.
I do not know about that. Other Ministers of Railways have said that but it did not work out.

I have made a few comparisons, but, as the hon. gentleman knows what I don't know about the Intercolonial railway would make a much bigger book than what I do know about it. I should think that if I undertook to teli this committee very much about the Intercolonial railway they would consider that I was rather bumptious. I have only been on the road once and then only on a part of the system, and the reason that I did not purpose making a general statement was that I would have to make it largely on what I have been told, not having had an opportunity, from personal experience, of studying the matter myself.

I represent one of the maritime provinces which is deeply interested in the operations of the Intercolonial railway and I fear I cannot agree either with the Minister of Railways or with the hon. member for Pictou.
I would not expect you to.

I think myself that if the Intercolonial railway in charging fair and reasonable rates to the people, which the people of the maritime provinces are quite willing to pay, earns a surplus, it is to the credit of the management of that railway. I think it is better for the lower provinces that such surplus should be shown, because when there is no surplus on the Intercolonial railway it has been the practice of persons coming from other parts of Canada to speak of the railway rather as a dead weight upon the people of Canada and to deciare that it ought to be got rid of as soon as possible and handed over to some private company.
That would not hurt very much.
Well I think it would. I am very strongly in favour of the Intercolonial railway being kept, owned1, and operated as a government railway.
Hear, hear.
Do you not think it ought to go into rolling stock ?

If you put all the surplus into betterments without treating it 'as a surplus, you do not give the government railway ia fair show, and you add to the 'argument of those who say that it is run at a loss to the people of Canada and that the sooner we get rid of it the better. We ought to make up our minds firmly to hold on to 'the Intercolonial railway forever, to be operated in the interest of the people of Canada.
How much has been charged up to capital in the operation of [DOT] the Intercolonial railway during the present fiscal year ?
The hon. minister is, I 'am sure, anxious to meet requests of this kind.
We have not heard from him.	.
Will the'hon. minister kindlv communicate with Mr. Savoie, who is one of the largest manufacturers along the line?

There has been a good deal of difficulty in getting the cars back from the United States, where the congestion is worse than it is in Canada. In November we had a number of complaints of the shortage of cars for the shipment of lumber and pulipwood, and Mr. Tiffin told me that an. enormous number of our cars were in the United States, and that he was trying to get them back.
Is there not a fine imposed for retaining these cars?

There is a fine of 35 cents a day, which the railway companies would rather pay and keep the cars. In regard to the expenditure on capital account, the auditor tells me that during the past year to the 1st of September it amounted to $1,156,207.

My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) looks at this matter from an entirely different standpoint from those of us who come from the province of Nova Scotia. The province of New Brunswick is fortunate enough to have two transcontinental systems, the Canadian Pacific railway running into the city of St. John and the Grand Trunk Pacific, which is completed to the city of Moncton, as wall as the Intercolonial. That pUovince is -therefore very fortunate in having plenty of railway accommodation which I do not begrudge it in the slightest degree. But in the province of Nova Scotia we have but one railway, giving us communication with the outside world, that is, the Intercolonial, and we have none of the transcontinental systems; and when we want additional railway 'accommodation w-e are compelled to come to- the Minister of Railways and- -ask him to build a branch line. My hon. friend now -tells us: You must show us that 'this is going to make money for the country or we will not talk about a branch line.
I did not say make money, I said pay its way.

The minister's expression is practically one which means what I said. I only want to point out-and I do not want to continue the discussion tonight, because it is now pretty late-that the member from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), certainly views this question from an entirely different standpoint to that from which I am compelled to view it. I would Mr. LEMIEUX.	!i
suggest to the minister that there is no desire on the part of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to do -other than discuss these estimates fairly, and, in view of the absence of a number of our friends who wish to speak upon these items, he ought not, perhaps, to proceed further to-night

I am perfectly willing and it will be certainly, a pleasure to furnish all the information as we go along, but I think we ought, to pass a few items before the committee rises.
Ajir-brakes-To improve triple values of $7,150.
Perhaps the minister would tell us what this vote for airbrakes is foil-?

The object of these airbrakes is to improve the feature known as quick service. The K triple valve has additional features, known as quick service uniform rails, and uniform recharge to meet modern conditions of freight service, using less air and being far superior for controlling trains on heavy grades, and is being adopted by a large number of railways. I might say that there was spent last year for the same purpose $3,314.16. The work is done by the staff. These cost about $5.50 each, and the estimate _ this year was to put these brakes on 1,300 frieght cars. It is only following out the policy which has been adopted in the past.

There have been reports in the newspapers that the minister contemplated some radical changes, in the board of management of the Intercolonial, I would like to know if he has any information to give the House as to his policy in that regard?
I have not seen any of the newspapers which gave currency to such reports, and I have no information to give.
Will the minister say whether any changes are contemplated?
I have no information m reference to the matter.
That is a very unsatisfactory answer to my question, for the minister to state that he has no information to give.	.
I can only repeat that answer.

This railway board was constituted after a great deal of deliberation, and its maintenance became the settled policy of the late government. The board has done very good work, and has been of great service to the country. The minister surely knows whether he intends to continue that board or not, and I should

think ought to be in a position to give us some information.
When the government has made up its mind to change the board it will be very glad to take the House into its confidence.
Does that mean that the government has not made up its mind at the present time to make any change?

Hon. gentlemen draw their own conclusions anyway, no matter what I say and they are at liberty to do the same in this instance.
Bridges-to strengthen, $100,000.
Where are these bridges to be strengthened?

It is hoped by means of this vote to complete the strengthening of the bridges on the main line of the Intercolonial, and afterwards to proceed with the strengthening of the bridges on the Cape Breton branch.
In the system of bookkeeping are the two items of betterments and maintenance kept separately, or are they under the heading of maintenance simply?

I understand it is a capital and revenue account.

I received a deputation from both Newcastle and Chatham this last week, and the matter I considered should stand until the proper place was selected where the bridge would be most useful for the country and the railway as well.

The minister refers to the question as to whether the wharf should be located at Chatham or Newcastle. For my own part I cannot see what in the world that would have to do with the vote in the estimates of last year. They are diverting the railway and taking it along the water front. The northwest wind blows very heavily on that side of the river and of course the boom must be filled in. The plans

Would the Minister be able to give the average expenditure on maintenance during say the last four years? I mean a comparison of the amounts expended on the road for maintenance per mile per year during that period?
Chatham-diversion of line and branch to wharf, $160,000.
seemed to me when I was Minister of Public Works that in order to make the branch railways into the town of Chatham of real service to the business people of that place, it was necessary to build a wharf and I had an item of $100,000 placed in the estimates for the purpose of doing that. When the estimates for the Public Works Department were under consideration I called the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the fact that the item of $100,000 had been left out, and if I remember rightly he was not able to tell me what was the intention in regard to it. Has the Minister of Railways com sidered the matter, and does he intend to use any part of this amount of $160,000 tor the terminals, including the wharf, or is it wholly apart from that, and if not what is my hon. friend's intention in regard to the construction of a railway wharf there?
I may say there is not in the amount of $160,000 anything for the wharf.' There has been a good deal of 132i

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I desire to ask a question for information. Where do the ocean steamers that now load deals at Chatham load?
A large number of ocean steamers load at the wharfs of the timber merchants, but large quantities of deals arriving over the road at present are loaded at the wharf known as the Canada dock.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is that a government wharf? Does it belong to the railway?

Yes. At that dock there is room for only one steamer to load at a time, and often there are steamers with coal for the railway to be unloaded at the same wharf. So, it was considered very important that, when they were constructing this road across this boom, instead of making the front of it of ripTap stone, it should be made of timber. At the time, I did not think it would cost much more- to make it of timber than of stone. It is possible a wharf more cheaply constructed might serve the purpose as well as a wharf built according to the plans prepared1. The very object of diverting the railway to the front of the town was to have shipping facilities, and hon. gentlemen know that success in shipping timber depends largely upon the ease with which it is handled. I would like it very much if the minister would favourably consider my suggestion,

and take up the matter with the Public Works Department, and, if reasonable at all, have a wharf of the dimensions proposed; or, if the cost is considered to be too much, then make plans for a cheaper wharf. What the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), said1 is true, that this expenditure was to be made by the Public Works Department for the use of the railway, but to be the property of the Public Works Department. In fact, I think it is the policy of the Railway Department in regard to other wharfs, viz., to hand them over to Public Works Department.	*
Does the hon. gen-'fleman mean that the side of the railway next the stream was to be constructed so that it could be used as a loading wharf?
Yes, but if stone were used that could not be done.
I desire to tell the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) that I will have the statement he asks for made to-morrow, so far as we .can make it.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will take up Bills and resolutions as far as possible.

speechtext:
So I understood. Then we will take up other Bills as far as it may be convenient to hon. members on the other side, and then resume in Supply, with the estimates of the Minister of Railways and Canals.
